1:
The feast is named before the plot. Chrysostom makes the Jewish actions a shadow of our own: ask a Jew what the Passover means and he tells you only of the deliverance from Egypt, whereas the Christian hears not of Egypt or Pharaoh but of freedom from sin and the darkness of Satan, wrought not by Moses but by the Son of God. Bede notes that the name comes not from the Passion but from the passing over. Gill takes the seven days of unleavened bread as a memorial of the haste in which Israel left Egypt, with no time to leaven the dough, and as a figure of the sincerity and truth of the gospel feast. Robertson observes that strictly the passover was Nisan the fourteenth and the unleavened bread the fifteenth to the twenty-first, and that the full phrase occurs only here in the New Testament. Henry sees the year of the redeemed arriving in its first month, so much in haste was the Redeemer, and in the very month in which God brought Israel out by Moses, that the antitype might answer the type.

Tertullian presses the choice of that feast against those who would part Christ from the law. He knew the time it behoved him to suffer, since the law prefigured his passion, and of all the festal days chose the one in which Moses had declared a sacred mystery. What a destroyer of the law was this, who longed to keep its passover; was he so fond of Jewish lamb, or was it because he had to be led like a lamb to the slaughter? He might have been betrayed by a stranger and without a price, but Jeremiah had named both the price and the potter's field.

On the plotters all agree. Henry has the chief priests, men of sanctity, and the scribes, men of learning, seeking how to kill him by force or fraud, and stopped only by their fear of the people. Gill adds the elders, making up the sanhedrim, and puts the meeting in the palace of Caiaphas. Bede judges that they feared not sedition but that by the interference of the people he should be taken out of their hands. Clarke holds that the mass of the people were convinced he was at least a prophet sent from God, and that the multitude clamouring for his blood at the crucifixion was a mere mob formed out of the creatures of the priests. Robertson finds the imperfect describing the delay: it was the how that stalled them, the triumphal entry and the temple speeches having shown his power with the crowds.

Then the door opened from inside. Theophylact marks the transition, the evangelist having said they sought a way without danger and now relating the way that offered itself. Titus of Bostra says Satan entered Judas not by force but finding the door open, since Judas, forgetful of all he had seen, had turned wholly to covetousness; one of the twelve is added because he made up the number without discharging the office. Bede reconciles John's later notice by distinguishing an entry as a stranger from one as his own. Barnes denies that Satan entered the body personally and makes it an influence on a besetting passion, avarice, the tempter commonly working by raising a man's own passions to their highest pitch; Robertson has Judas opening the door himself, with the surrender in no way relieving him of moral responsibility. Clarke turns it on the reader: a minister who loves money betrays the interests of Christ continually. Wesley adds only that Satan is never wanting to assist those whose heart is bent upon mischief. Lightfoot and Ellicott then dispute the captains, the one doubting that Roman officers of Antonia would be so called, the other making them the officers set over the Levite guardians, whose sentinels carried clubs.
7:
Titus of Bostra states the day's logic in a sentence: to leave us a heavenly Passover our Lord ate a typical one, removing the figure that the truth might take its place. Bede fixes the date as the fourteenth of the first month, when the leaven having been put away the lamb was held toward evening; Gill agrees. Clarke distinguishes the name of the festival from that of the sacrificed lamb on which they feasted. Robertson notes that the day itself came rather than merely drew nigh, that the lamb was slain by the head of the family, and that Luke, writing as a Gentile, presents as fact the reckoning the Synoptics share, which John rightly interpreted does not contradict. Henry draws the lesson: Christ was made under the law and kept its ordinances, the passover in particular, to teach us not to neglect his own gospel institutions.

Ellicott observes that Luke alone names the two sent, and finds a loving insight in an act that brought them together just when one would need the sympathy of the other. Theophylact names them as the loving and the loved, and says that to the very end of his life Christ opposed not the law; he sends them to a strange house because he and his disciples had none. Bede hears their question as a confession: we have no abode, no shelter. Let those hear it, he says, who busy themselves in building houses, and know that Christ, the Lord of all places, had nowhere to lay his head. Henry adds that Christ could have described the house, probably one they knew, and directed them by a sign instead to teach them to follow the conduct of Providence step by step, going without knowing whither they went; they need not fear disappointment who go upon Christ's word.

The sign is taken as evidence of two things at once. Ambrose bids us observe first the greatness of the divine power, that while talking with his disciples he knows what happens elsewhere, and next the condescension, in that he seeks out not the rich or powerful but the poor, preferring a mean inn to the spacious palaces of nobles; the man is left unnamed that he may be counted as ignoble. Theophylact takes the anonymity differently: he was sent to an unknown man to show that he underwent the Passion willingly, since one who could so sway a stranger's mind could have dealt with the Jews as he wished; though others, he reports, hold that the name was hidden from the traitor. Cyril of Alexandria says the same of the whole design: his right hand is almighty, yet he submitted of his own accord to taste death for the life of all, and the rebellious serpent, imagining he had prevailed, was disappointed of his expectation.

Over the pitcher and the upper room readings multiply. Bede has the Passover prepared in the house whither the water is carried, for the hour is at hand when the typical blood is taken from the lintel and the baptism of the life-giving fountain consecrated to take away sin. Origen keeps the man a real servant carrying water for washing or drinking, then reads him as Moses conveying spiritual doctrine in fleshly histories, and warns that those who follow him not, and those taken up with banquetings and worldly cares, neither ascend to the upper room nor keep the Passover with Jesus. Theophylact makes the water the grace of the Holy Spirit and the pitcher humbleness of heart, grace being given to the humble who know themselves earth and dust; Ambrose calls the pitcher a more perfect measure and the water that which was thought meet for a sacrament of Christ, to wash and not to be washed. Robertson, unmoved, notes the deliberative subjunctive in the disciples' question and the late word for the goodman of the house.
14:
Bede dates the hour to the fourteenth day far gone toward evening, the fifteenth moon just appearing; Gill puts it after six o'clock, at the last of the two evenings, Barnes simply at the hour of eating the paschal lamb. Robertson notes that the word for sitting down means reclining, and Theophylact meets the objection that the Jews ate the Passover standing by answering that when the legal Passover had been eaten they sat down by custom to the rest of their food.

On the doubled verb of desire philologists and preachers divide the labour. Ellicott calls the cognate noun a characteristically Hebrew idiom and infers that Luke heard the saying from someone repeating the very words spoken in Aramaic; Robertson adds that the construction is common in the Septuagint. Barnes supposes that Christ, about to leave them, wished once to see them together and to share one of the religious privileges of the Jewish dispensation, never having undervalued the rites of his country. Clarke makes it the longing of one who, having purposed to redeem a lost world by his blood, ardently desired the hour of offering himself up. Wesley divides the desire between the disciples, to whom he would manifest himself further at this parting, and the Church, for which he would institute the memorial of his death. Cyril of Alexandria gives the reason for the secrecy that made the meal possible: the covetous disciple was watching for a time to betray him, and neither the house nor the man had been divulged. Theophylact hears a farewell, as those going away utter their last words most affectionately, and Chrysostom that after this Passover the Cross was at hand.

What kingdom the Passover is fulfilled in is left open. Bede has Christ approving the legal Passover and then, having taught that it was the figure of his own dispensation, forbidding it to be kept in the flesh: he will celebrate it no more until, spiritually understood, it is fulfilled in the Church, which is the kingdom of God. Wesley puts the commencement at the resurrection, and Theophylact agrees that the resurrection is called the kingdom because it has destroyed death, Christ drinking again with his disciples to prove it no shadow. Clarke refers it to the death by which the kingdom was established, Ellicott to the cross and to every commemoration of it, each act being a communion with him as well as with one another, and Robertson to a Messianic banquet. Gill notes only that the passover, with the rest of the ceremonial law, was now to be abolished.

The cup before the institution is no part of it. Barnes says the sacramental cup came after supper, and that Christ, having kept this one in the usual manner, ingrafted the new ordinance on the old; Clarke pictures it passing from the first man on his right to the last on his left. Gill counts four cups which the poorest man in Israel was obliged to drink, and takes this for the first. Ellicott makes it the first of three added by Jewish custom, with a meaning of its own, and finds in the uncommon word for dividing an anticipation of the tongues parted at Pentecost. Calvin asks whether the two cups of this account are one thing told twice or two acts, and judges them two: the fathers observed a solemn rite of tasting the cup during sacrifices, and Christ kept it before turning to a mystery wholly unlike the paschal lamb. Robertson observes that the verb of thanksgiving here gives us the word Eucharist, and Bede that thanks were given because the old things were passing away and all becoming new. Chrysostom draws a table rule from it: satisfy hunger with moderation, since after the meal you must pray, and let food be followed not by sleep but by prayer and Scripture.
19:
Bede marks the hinge: the old Passover finished, Christ passes to the new, which he would have the Church celebrate in memory of his redemption, putting in place of the flesh and blood of the lamb the sacrament of his own under the figure of bread and wine, being made a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. He gave thanks here as at the close of the old feast, an example to glorify God at the beginning and end of every good work; and he breaks with his own hands the bread he holds out, to show that the breaking of his body will not be against his will. Gill notes that the account of the Lord's supper begins only here, the passover being eaten, and Wesley that it was after that supper ended.

Lightfoot finds the formula built on antithesis and allusion, since the Jews used the very phrase of the paschal lamb, bringing in the table with bitter herbs, unleavened bread and the body of the Passover; the sense is that by the same signification by which the lamb was my body hitherto, from henceforth let this bread be my body. Wesley reasons alike, that having just kept the supper called the passover Christ uses like figurative language of the bread, and that this alone was enough to prevent anyone supposing it his real body any more than the lamb was the passover. Gregory of Nyssa states the other side flatly: before the consecration it is common bread, but when the mystery has consecrated it, it is, and is called, the Body of Christ. Chrysostom presses what follows on the communicant: this blood moulds a royal image in us and opened heaven, yet a man polluted by an evil conscience comes to his own destruction, for if those who defile the imperial purple are punished like those who tear it, it is not unreasonable that they who receive Christ with an unclean heart should be beaten with the stripes of those who pierced him.

Calvin fastens on the clause the other evangelists omit: the flesh of Christ is life-giving because by it salvation was once procured, so that whoever would be nourished by it must look at it as offered on the cross to be the price of our reconciliation with God. Henry keeps the memorial in view, the breaking of bread reminding us of the breaking of his body as a sacrifice, and nothing being more nourishing to the soul than an atonement made and an interest in it assured. Robertson thinks the verses genuine though some manuscripts omit them, and observes that the true text elsewhere reads which is for you, not which is broken for you; the command is a present imperative of repetition.

Theophylact counts the two cups, the first a type of the Old Testament and the second imparted after the bread, and hears the Lord call this one the New Testament. Ellicott prefers the rendering covenant, noting that the adjective and the shed for you are alike peculiar to Luke in the best manuscripts, the participle being present, is being shed, like the being given before it. Clarke paraphrases the cup as signifying the blood of the new covenant shortly to be ratified by the shedding of his own, and remarks that Christ handed the elements to the man next him to be passed along, so that the present mode of administration departs from the institution. Wesley calls it an undeniable figure, the cup standing for the wine in it, and the New Testament in his blood meaning not the covenant but its seal and sign. Cyril of Jerusalem sets the table of the psalm against another: before Christ's coming the evil spirits had prepared a polluted table, and God has now spread this mystical one over against it, the one having communion with devils and the other with God.
21:
Whether Judas received the sacrament is the sharpest disagreement here, and it turns on where the saying stands. Lightfoot asks what more could be desired to show that Judas was present at the eucharist, and dismisses the contrary argument from John as making something out of nothing, since there is not a syllable there of the paschal supper but only of a supper before the feast. Henry reaches the same conclusion from the order, Luke placing the words after the institution where the other two place them before, so that Judas did eat of that bread and drink of that cup; there have been those who ate bread with Christ and betrayed him. Wesley denies it flatly: Christ spoke before the institution, since the other evangelists put the sop immediately before Judas went out, and the sop could not be given except while the meat was on the table, which was removed before the bread and cup came. Robertson records the difference without deciding it, Luke narrating the institution before the exposure where Mark and Matthew reverse the order; the participle has Judas actually engaged in the act, his hand on the table.

The fathers take the announcement as instruction, not accusation. Augustine notes that it was after giving the cup that Christ spoke again of his betrayer. Theophylact says it was made not only to show that Christ knew all things but to declare his goodness, since he left nothing undone that belonged to him, giving us an example that to the end we should be reclaiming sinners; it exposes besides a traitor who blushed not to be his guest. Chrysostom presses further: partaking of the mystery, he was not converted, and his wickedness is the more awful, since he came under the pollution of such a design and was made no better by fear, gratitude or respect. Bede notes that our Lord does not name him, lest being detected he grow the more shameless, but throws the charge on the whole twelve so that the guilty one might repent, and proclaims the punishment so that one whom shame had not moved might be amended.

Tertullian turns the woe into an argument. It must be the imprecation of an angry Master, unless Judas was to escape with impunity after so vast a sin. And if Christ knowingly let a man he had chosen for a companion plunge into so great a crime, the argument brought against the Creator in Adam's case recoils on those who bring it, who must charge their own God with ignorance, or inability, or unwillingness to hinder the sinner he foresaw.

On the determinate counsel both halves are kept. Gill glosses the going simply as dying, the way of all the earth, and Clarke observes that the best Greek and Latin writers use the words for going away in that sense. Ellicott notes that the word rendered determined is characteristic of Luke, and that the woe, standing in all three of the first Gospels, is among the sayings that made an indelible impression, reproduced word for word amid many variations. Robertson adds that the fact does not absolve Judas of the guilt the woe makes plain. Henry says the same: Christ was not driven to his sufferings but went cheerfully, and neither the patience of the saints nor the counsel of God will excuse those who have a hand in them. Theophylact had put it that he went not as unable to preserve himself but as determining to suffer death for man's salvation.

Gill remarks that at Bethany two days before the same hint had left them looking at one another, unable to speak, whereas now they inquire; and Basil, on their asking after a sin they were not conscious of, compares the diseases of the body which the sufferer does not feel, so that he trusts his physician rather than his own insensibility.
24:
Theophylact traces the quarrel to the question just asked: inquiring which of them should betray him, they would pass to saying you are the traitor, and thence to I am the greatest. Barnes finds nothing more humiliating than that, while Jesus contemplated his own death, they should contend about office and rank; Robertson, glossing the rare noun as an eagerness to contend, calls it the tragedy of the situation, the Cross before him and the traitor at the table. Whether it belongs here at all is disputed. Clarke identifies it with the dispute occasioned by the request of Zebedee's wife, recorded here out of order; Wesley agrees; Gill reports the same suspicion while noting a version which pins it to this moment. Ellicott holds the incident peculiar to Luke.

On the title of benefactor philology carries the argument. Barnes denies that Christ condemns the authority of kings as such, and observes that the word was applied to them by flattery, above all to the Roman emperors. Clarke notes that the Greek word was the surname of some of the Ptolemies, and that Rome gave conquered lands to her soldiers, called thence beneficiaries, so that oppressive sovereigns were called benefactors by men living on their bounty. Ellicott finds the emphasis falling on are called, as against the let him become that follows, the world giving the name to those great in power only. Wesley puts it shortest: they that exercise the most arbitrary authority have from their flatterers the vain title of benefactors.

Lightfoot presses that the younger is properly a term of age, and asks who will deny that Peter was the oldest, which would explain his standing first in the catalogue and sitting next the Lord. Clarke follows him and places the strife between Peter and the sons of Zebedee. Ellicott hears the words as half technical already, the younger carrying the idea of service, he that is chief standing near to presbyter, and the verb of serving giving us deacon. Ambrose warns that not every deference betokens humility, since a man may defer from fear of power or regard to his own interest, and so edify himself rather than honour another; the precept for all is that they boast not of precedence but strive for humility. Bede adds that the great need judgment here, neither tyrannising like the kings of the Gentiles nor puffed up with praise, yet zealous against offenders. Robertson states the rule flatly, that true greatness is in service, not rank, and hears behind the words the washing of the feet that same evening.

Theophylact marks the turn, woe having been denounced on the traitor and blessing being now promised to the rest; Bede that not the first effort of patience but long perseverance is crowned, perseverance being the pillar of all virtues. Ellicott argues that the temptations cannot be the Temptation but must be the trials of the ministry; Robertson prefers trials likewise, and Calvin takes them for the contests by which God tried Master and apostles in common, Christ's own faith and patience being actually tried. Calvin finds in the example a call to patience, since though ordained a King he was not at once raised to glory but won kingly honour by the ignominy of the cross. Ellicott notes that the verb of appointing gives us the word covenant, so the promise was part of the new covenant with them, while Clarke records a reading which puts covenant for kingdom. Gill takes the kingdom as spiritual, the government of the church committed to apostles; Wesley insists it is not a primacy to one but a kingdom to every one alike; Cyril of Alexandria explains that spiritual things are described by present ones, since those who sit at an earthly king's table enjoy a high privilege; and Ambrose adds that the reward promised is not food and drink but heavenly grace and life.
31:
Bede reads the warning as a check on the praise just given: lest the eleven impute to their own strength that they almost alone had continued with him, Christ shows that without his aid the same storm would have beaten them down, and that no man's faith is tried unless God permits it. Clarke says a repeated name is love speaking in a warning voice, and insists from the plural pronoun that the words were not for Peter alone, Satan having got Judas, nearly got Peter, and wishing to have all; the devil is permitted only some of the evil he desires. Gill notes that Christ uses not the name he had given, which signified firmness, but the older one, doubled to show earnestness and concern. Ellicott hears in the doubling the emphasis of sadness, and finds both verbs in a tense treating the act as wholly past, as though the Lord had stood in some scene like the opening of Job and prevailed by his intercession. Robertson glosses the first verb as begging for oneself and the second from the winnowing fan; Barnes compares the giving of Job into Satan's hands.

Why Peter is singled out divides them. Theophylact says it was because he was bolder than the rest and might grow proud of Christ's promises, Ellicott because the disciple most confident of his greatness stood in most danger. Lightfoot turns the verse against the use made of it: change the name to Thomas or Philip, and who would have drawn from it an argument for their primacy over the universal Church? Yet this the Romanists do for Peter, when the words are a severe chiding.

Chrysostom observes that he says not I have granted but I have prayed, speaking humbly as one approaching his Passion, since he who said with authority that on this rock he would build his Church needed no prayer to steady one soul; nor is it I have prayed that you deny not, but that you do not abandon your faith. Clarke presses that Peter's faith failed but not utterly, and that he fell without falling off as Judas did. Barnes takes faith here for attachment to Christ and the failing for total apostasy, and reasons that since God always heard his Son there was no moment when Peter was not a pious man. Robertson concludes that Jesus could not keep Satan from attacking Peter but could pray for his faith, the participle of turning again implying the fall; Ellicott, that faith did fail at the denial, yet repentance and a new power to strengthen others followed. Wesley reads the charge as addressed to all that are weak in faith.

Ambrose finds Peter earnest in spirit but weak in bodily inclination and unable to match the constancy of the divine will, our Lord's Passion having rivals but no equal; Theophylact draws the doctrine that human resolve is not sufficient without divine support. Basil adds that God sometimes allows the rash to fall as a remedy for their self-confidence, the man who sins almost against his will differing greatly from those who care neither for themselves nor for God. Calvin finds Luke's version fuller, since Christ does not narrate the coming trouble but declares that they will have a contest with Satan and promises them the victory. Cyril of Alexandria sounds the summons to be awake, since the enemy seizes our passions to lead us on to a reprobate mind, and those who would not be subject to him conquer by Christ's help. Augustine notes that Matthew and Mark place the warning after the company left the house and Luke and John before it, and that the differences compel us to think Peter boasted three times and was three times answered. Ellicott hears in that boast a latent indignation as well as devotion, Robertson that Peter, unflattered by such prayers, answered with a loud claim.
35:
The appeal to their first mission is a deliberate contrast. Cyril of Alexandria sets it just after the warning to Peter: having spoken of his being taken captive, Christ announces the struggle to follow. Chrysostom illustrates the change by a swimming master, who at first holds his pupils up with his hands and afterwards withdraws them, bidding them help themselves and even letting them sink a little. Bede states the rule: Christ does not train his disciples by the same discipline in persecution as in peace, and when the whole nation persecuted shepherd and flock he proposed a law suited to the time, leaving us an example that when a just reason urges we may without blame relax something of the strictness of a resolve. Augustine adds that this is no inconsistency in him who commands but the reason of a dispensation. Ellicott finds evidence that on that first journey they were welcomed and wanted nothing; Barnes, that Christ recalls it to convince them from their own experience; Calvin, that he had kept them in the shade like children so that, courage gathered, they might now labour like men.

The sword divides everyone. Ambrose asks why he who forbids to strike should order them to buy one, and answers that there may be a defence prepared but no necessary retaliation, a seeming ability to be revenged without the will. Chrysostom asks how he who said turn the other cheek can now arm them, and with a sword only, when a completely armed man would need shield and helmet, and a thousand such weapons would not fit eleven men to face whole nations. Calvin makes it figurative, a general calling soldiers to arms so that everything must be sold to buy weapons, yet warning them under that comparison of the struggles of temptation they must sustain. Lightfoot answers that it is common speech, the rabbins using the like of selling a garment to buy oil for the feast of Dedication, and that Christ warns them of a near danger, to give them such an apprehension of their enemies' rage as would suppress their private animosities. Clarke reports Pearce's suspicion that the word sword was inserted here from the later verse. Wesley says shortly that the words are plainly not literal and mean only a time of extreme danger. Robertson allows a defensive sense but denies that force is to be repelled by force.

Over the prophecy Barnes distinguishes carefully, that Christ was reckoned not as a transgressor but among them, put to death in their company and treated as such though holy and undefiled. Calvin makes the adverb emphatic, since Christ had not discharged every part of his office until he was ranked with the wicked as if of their class. Ellicott finds the citation remarkable as showing that the picture of the righteous sufferer had been present all along to our Lord's thoughts; Lightfoot glosses the closing clause as meaning that his business is done and theirs only beginning, which is no time for contending with one another, and Clarke reproduces that gloss as his own.

At the two swords the irony is general. Gill has the disciples taking the words literally, the swords perhaps brought from Galilee against the robbers who infested the road, and asking whether these were sufficient; Barnes and Wesley both note that Galileans commonly travelled armed for that reason. Robertson observes that before the night is out Peter will use one of these very swords and be sternly rebuked, so that Christ plainly did not mean the language pressed too literally, and dismisses the subject with sad irony. Ellicott hears the same grave irony, two swords being enough and more than enough for one who did not mean them used at all, and rejects, as Calvin does, the reading which finds in them the spiritual and temporal authority of Peter and his successors.
39:
Bede observes that, being about to be betrayed by his own disciple, our Lord goes to the place of his wonted retirement, where he might most easily be found; Robertson says the same from the other side, that Judas dared the betrayal without waiting for the crowds because he knew the habit. Cyril of Alexandria sets the rhythm of those days, that by day he was in Jerusalem and when darkness came he held converse with his disciples on the mount of Olives; Gill has him leaving the upper room and the city together, to begin his sufferings without the camp; Clarke and Wesley name Gethsemane. Ellicott notes that the long discourses of the fourth Gospel belong here.

Theophylact marks what he does with the night: after supper he betakes himself not to idleness or sleep but to prayer and teaching. Bede weighs the form of the charge: since it is impossible for the soul of man not to be tempted, he says not pray that you be not tempted but pray that you enter not into temptation, that the temptation may not at last overcome you. Robertson presses the tense, keep on praying not to enter, not even once, and holds this real temptation and not merely trial, so that the words light up the petition of the Lord's Prayer. Cyril of Alexandria observes that you will everywhere find him praying apart, to teach us to speak with the most high God with a quiet heart, though he did not pray as one wanting help, being himself the almighty power of the Father. Ellicott hears in the stone's cast a touch implying a report from an eyewitness, peculiar to Luke, and finds the tense implying continuous prayer.

Gregory of Nyssa asks what the bending of the knees means. Men pray to their superiors with faces to the ground; yet since human nature contains nothing worthy of God's imitation, so that the tokens of respect we show one another we have transferred to the humiliation of the incomparable Nature. He who bore our sicknesses bent his knee by reason of the manhood he assumed, an example against exalting ourselves at the time of prayer. Chrysostom denies that the petition can be a confession of ignorance or a refusal, since the Father's pleasure was no harder to know than the Father's substance, and since he had rebuked as Satan a disciple who wished to prevent his Passion. Athanasius finds here a double will, one human and of the flesh, which through weakness refuses the Passion, the other divine, which eagerly embraced it; and Gregory of Nyssa turns that against Apollinaris, who allowed Christ no will of his own according to his earthly nature, asking what will it can then be that God would by no means have fulfilled.

Over the cup Bede offers a reading of his own, that Christ begs its removal not from fear of suffering but from compassion for the first people, lest they should drink the cup he drank first: he says not remove the cup but this cup, the cup of a people who can plead no ignorance in slaying him. Gill supplies the condition as a consistency with the declared will of saving sinners, where the others put a possibility. Ellicott hears an echo of the prayer Christ had taught, since he too could say lead us not into temptation, subject now to the Father's will being done; Robertson notes the present imperative, keep on being done. Henry sets the whole scene under the making of his soul an offering for sin, in which he afflicted his own soul with grief for the sin he was to satisfy for and with an apprehension of the wrath of God; in it he entered the lists with the powers of darkness, gave them every advantage they could desire, and conquered them still.
43:
Theophylact takes the angel as a lesson in the power of prayer, that we may exercise it in adversity. Bede reads the visit as a testimony to both natures, since angels are said both to have ministered to him and to have comforted him, the Creator needing no protection from his creature, but being made man he is sad and comforted for our sakes; Chrysostom adds that because he took our flesh in reality he submits to bear human things. Barnes meets the objection that an angel's comfort would disprove his divinity: the human nature was in agony, and it is God's manner to sustain the afflicted by such intervention. Clarke argues that the fullest evidence had to be given of both natures, the miracles attesting one and the hunger and agony the other; Wesley adds, lest his body sink and die before the time. Gill declines to guess whether the angel was Michael or Gabriel, holding only that it was a good one in visible form; Robertson notes that angels came after the three temptations, this one during the conflict. Ellicott records that not a few of the best manuscripts omit these verses though the balance of evidence favours them, and that the angel appeared to our Lord only.

On the sweat the vocabulary is itself evidence. Ellicott notes that the noun describes a conflict rather than physical pain, and that the four words Luke uses here occur nowhere else in the New Testament and are such as a medical writer would use. Robertson glosses the drops as thick clotted blood, a word common in medical works, notes the absence of the passage from some ancient documents, and cites Aristotle on a bloody sweat. Clarke says the word for agony points out the utmost anguish of soul, and rejects as unlikely the softer reading that only the size of the drops is meant; Theophylact had offered just that reading, since it is proverbially said of a man who has sweated intensely that he sweated blood.

What caused it divides them sharply. Gill makes the agony a conflict with the devil, now appearing visibly in a horrible form: after the wilderness Satan left him for a season, and now the prince of this world attacked him in a garden, where the first onset on human nature was made. Wesley has him grappling with the powers of darkness, feeling the weight of the wrath of God and surrounded by a host of devils. Lightfoot refuses that account outright: he dare not imagine that God was angry or conceived any indignation against him at all, and ascribes the bloody sweat to the bite of that old serpent rather than to any apprehension of divine wrath, citing Diodorus on serpents whose bite brings an issue of sweat like blood. Augustine leaves the cause aside and reads the sign: our Lord praying with a bloody sweat represented the martyrdoms which should flow from his whole body, the Church.

The sleep is excused before being rebuked. Chrysostom observes that it was midnight and their eyes were heavy from grief, their sleep being not of drowsiness but of sorrow; Ellicott finds it characteristic of Luke that where the others state the fact he assigns the cause, prolonged sorrow having a numbing effect; Robertson, that Luke does not tell of the three turnings to the trusted three. Bede holds that what follows proves Christ had been praying for the disciples, whom he now exhorts to be partakers of it by watching and prayer. Theophylact glosses the charge: not to be led into temptation is not to be overwhelmed by it; or else he bids us pray that our life may be quiet, since it is presumptuous for a man to throw himself into temptation. Augustine ends where the harmonist must, noting that Luke has not stated after which prayer Christ came to his disciples.
47:
The Gloss marks the turn, that having told of the prayer Luke goes on to the betrayal by his own disciple. Cyril of Alexandria hears contempt in the phrasing, since the evangelist says he that was called Judas as though holding the name in abhorrence, and adds one of the twelve to signify the enormity, one honoured as an apostle becoming the cause of the murder of Christ. Robertson notes that Judas went in front, leading the band because he knew the place well. Henry sets the scene in a longer war: Satan, baffled in his attempt to terrify our Lord and put him out of possession of his own soul, betakes himself to force and arms and brings a party into the field. Gill marks only the moment, while he yet spake.

Henry follows the sign: they did not know which was he, so Judas told them that whomsoever he kissed was the man, and drew near according to that wonted freedom to which our Lord admitted his disciples. Must the badge of friendship be made the instrument of treachery, he asks, and was ever a love-token so abused? Cyril of Alexandria says the same, that unmindful of Christ's glory he thought to act secretly, daring to make a token of love the instrument of treason. Chrysostom explains why nothing had stopped him: as incurable wounds yield neither to severe nor to soothing remedies, so a soul once sold to some particular sin reaps no benefit from admonition, and so it was with Judas, whom every warning had failed to deter. Ambrose takes the words that follow as a question in which he arrests the traitor with a lover's affection: do you inflict a wound with the pledge of love? Chrysostom adds that he gives him his proper name like one lamenting and recalling him rather than provoked to anger.

Ambrose finds in the title a whole argument. Here is a great manifestation of divine power and a great discipline of virtue, that the traitor's design is detected and yet forbearance is not withheld; by manifesting what was hidden he shows whom Judas betrays, and by saying the Son of man declares whom he delivers up, since it is the human flesh and not the divine nature that is seized. What most confounds the ungrateful is that he had delivered up one who, being the Son of God, for our sakes wished to be the Son of man. And our Lord returned the kiss, not to teach us to dissemble, but that he might not seem to shrink from the traitor and might move him the more by not denying him the offices of love. Augustine orders the three sayings, Luke's first, then Matthew's, then John's.

Lightfoot studies the traitor's mind. Our Saviour had to do with a frightful and terrifying devil, he says, but this man seems possessed with a tame and gentle one: he converses with the apostles with no token of a devil dwelling in him, and is present at the Passover, at the eucharist, at the very lips of Christ, with no sign of Satan being his inmate; but when once the devil has done his work by a man, let him take heed of his devil.

Theophylact turns to the disciples, inflamed with zeal and unsheathing their swords: whence had they swords at all, unless because they had slain the lamb and were come from the feast? The others ask whether they should strike, but Peter, always fervent for his Master, waits for no permission. Bede gives the last word of the scene: the Lord is never forgetful of his loving kindness, and while they bring death upon the righteous he heals the wounds of his persecutors.
48:
Gill hears the name itself as reproach: he calls him Judas that he might know he was known: my apostle, my friend, my familiar friend in whom I trusted. Barnes makes every word emphatic: dost thou violate all thy obligations of fidelity, thou who hast been so long with him and so much favoured, and betray the Son of man, the hope of the nations? Clarke asks whether he kisses him as a friend while delivering him to his enemies, and says we need not wonder, since Satan had entered his heart. Ellicott notes that the first three Gospels record the kiss but Luke alone the question, and traces a twofold purpose in the title, the familiar name appealing to memory and conscience and the name of the Judge and King warning the traitor of his own retribution. Robertson observes that Jesus challenges the act openly and calls it betrayal, and that it did not stop him; Wesley reads the question as turning on knowledge, he whom thou knowest to be the Son of man. Cyril of Jerusalem, gathering the testimonies of the Passion, begins where it began, with a traitor who came and stood speaking words of peace but plotting war.

Ellicott finds the phrase for those who spoke more accurate than the disciples would have been, these being probably the three who had been nearest. Robertson notes that Luke alone gives their question and alone, as a physician, says the right ear, John following him and adding the names of Peter and Malchus, probably because both were dead by then; Gill takes those names from the same source. On the following words readings differ. Clarke suggests they may mean suffer me to go thus far, the crowd having a firm hold of Christ while he sought leave to reach Malchus and heal him. Ellicott leaves it open between the disciples and the officers, inclining to the latter because the immediate healing tends to conciliation. Robertson prefers the disciples, adding that this miracle of surgery is Luke's alone.

Calvin gives the healing another motive: Peter's foolish zeal had brought grievous reproach on his Master's doctrine, Satan contriving to involve the Gospel in eternal disgrace, as though Christ had kept company with assassins for revolutionary ends; that is why he healed the wound Peter had inflicted, though a fearful stupidity had seized adversaries whom the miracle left unmoved.

Gill has Christ turn to the chief priests only after the miracle had quieted the mob and kept them from cutting the apostles to pieces. Ellicott notes that Luke alone records the presence of men of higher rank with the officers, and prefers the rendering robber, with swords and clubs; Robertson says plainly that they were treating him as a bandit like Barabbas, and finds the surrender voluntary, they having taken undue advantage of an hour of secret prayer after failing to seize him in the temple. Wesley observes that the priests and captains and elders came of their own accord while the soldiers and servants were sent, and glosses the hour as the time before which they could not take him. Clarke makes the permission the whole point: this is the time in which they may unrein their malice, which they could not do before because God did not permit it, so perfectly are they under his control that neither they nor the prince of darkness can move a hair's breadth except by leave: a comfortable thought, he says, for the followers of Christ. Lightfoot presses the other side of the same hour: the serpent himself is come in Judas and the seed of the serpent is the rout with him, all fences lie open and the devil's chains are loosed, so that he may exert his furies at pleasure. Ellicott adds that in identifying the power working through human instruments with darkness our Lord virtually claims to be the Light.
54:
Ambrose guards the first clause: when we read that Jesus was holden, let us not think him holden in respect of his divine nature, or unwilling through weakness, for he is held captive according to the truth of his bodily nature. Gill notes that they laid hold of him notwithstanding the miracle he had just wrought, which was itself a confirmation of his last words, that now was their hour. Bede identifies the chief priest as Caiaphas, Augustine adding that he was first led to Annas, though Mark and Luke give no name; Robertson observes that Luke alone mentions the house. Chrysostom finds Peter's zeal in his not flying when all the others did, and adds that he rightly followed afar off, being soon to deny, for he could never have denied had he clung close to Christ, yet must be revered for not forsaking his Lord even in fear, since fear is the effect of nature and solicitude of tender affection. Henry is harder: the fall began in sneaking, for Peter followed, which showed concern, but afar off to be out of danger, thinking to trim the matter, satisfy his conscience and still save his reputation and sleep in a whole skin.

Gill explains the fire, since it was cold in the night even at the passover, the servants kindling it in the middle of the hall while Jesus was examined at the other end. Ellicott prefers court-yard to hall, our word suggesting a covered space indoors, and notes that the phrase is literally by the light; Robertson glosses the verb as kindling a fire that blazes all round, it being April and cool at night. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson agree that the maid gazed steadily, the word being one of Luke's favourites, and Ellicott adds that John's narrative explains why she said this man also. Gill has Peter, startled at her assertion, deny roundly at once, so that the man who said he would die with his Master is frighted by a servant maid.

Robertson doubts the denials in the four accounts can be co-ordinated unless several joined in when one led off, and notes that each tangles Peter further. Wesley harmonises them by distributing the charge: the maid who led him in first put the question and then affirmed it, another accused him to the bystanders and gave occasion to the man here mentioned. Ellicott notes that the vocative rendered Man always implies anger or impatience, and that the phrase for an hour having intervened and the word for confidently affirmed are alike peculiar to Luke; Wesley remarks that in all that hour Peter did not recollect himself.

Chrysostom bids us marvel at the Master, who though a prisoner had such forethought for his disciple that by a look he brought him to himself and provoked him to tears. Augustine warns that this needs care, since Peter was outside in the court while the trial went on within, so that the looking seems to have been done in a divine manner; Ellicott places the glance where it can be seen, our Lord being led from Annas to the public trial, and calls it the turning point of Peter's life, mentioned by Luke alone. Bede reads the hour: Peter who sinned at midnight repented at cock-crow, correcting by remembrance of the true light the error committed in the darkness of forgetfulness; and Christ is denied not only by the man who says he is not the Christ but by the Christian who says he is not one. Clarke reports that Peter's name is omitted in the last verse by many good manuscripts, and Robertson that a few old Latin documents omit the verse, though the evidence is too slight. Cyril of Alexandria finds that many bitter passions war with the soul, but worst is the love of money, into whose inextricable nets the traitor fell.
63:
Augustine notes that the mockings and Peter's temptation are not related by all the evangelists in the same order, Matthew and Mark putting the mockings first and Luke the denial; Clarke marks the same displacement, Wesley suggesting that Christ was abused in the same manner both before and after his condemnation. Chrysostom sets the scene in a word: the Lord of heaven and earth suffers the mockings of the ungodly, giving us an example of patience. Theophylact adds that the Lord of prophets is derided as a false prophet, and that they blindfolded him not that he should not see their wickedness but that they might hide his face from them. Henry presses the cruelty, that the servants allowed him no rest though he had had no sleep all night, and made his sorrowful night their merriment, the blessed Jesus, like Samson, made the fool in the play. Robertson notes that the verb for holding is used here alone of a prisoner and that the imperfect is inchoative, they began to mock like boys; Gill has the men either soldiers or the high priest's servants, gripping him lest he escape, though his time was come. Ellicott traces the taunt to a popular Judaism that identified prophecy with clairvoyance; Wesley turns the charge round, since they accused him of blasphemy because he said he was the Son of God, while the evangelist fixes that charge on them, because he really was so.

Robertson observes that this is the second appearance before the Sanhedrin, which Mark and Matthew merely mention, and that the word for the assembly is the technical term for the eldership. Ellicott records what Luke passes over, the false witnesses who did not agree and the silence until the adjuration, the answer about their unbelief being Luke's alone. Theophylact says he knew the secrets of their hearts: those who had not believed his works would much less believe his words. Bede recalls that he had often declared himself the Christ, and had asked how they called the Christ David's son when David called him Lord, though they would neither believe nor answer. Clarke puts it bluntly, that even if they could give no answer they would not let him go, since he knew they were determined on his death.

Theophylact hears the answer as closing the discourse: no time is left for teaching, but hereafter comes judgment. Ellicott renders it from this time forth shall the Son of man be sitting, and admits that in Luke's record the confession follows the apparent refusal with hardly any consistency, Matthew showing the change to have been caused by the high priest's adjuration; Clarke takes the word to mean that from this very time the kingdom of God is to be set up. Bede notes that they understood him to call himself the Son of God, Ambrose that the Lord had rather prove himself a King than call himself one, that they might have no excuse for condemning him when they confess the truth of what they lay against him. Robertson holds that Jesus answers their demand about the Messiah by asserting that he is the Son of man, the three titles being practical equivalents, so that he admits all three.

Cyril of Alexandria notes that at this the Pharisees were very wroth and uttered shameful words. Theophylact draws the moral, that the disobedient gain nothing when the more secret mysteries are revealed to them but rather incur the heavier punishment, so that such things ought to be concealed. Gill has the whole sanhedrim speaking with one voice, greedy to lay hold of the words; Clarke observes that they had gone as far as they could, the Jews having no power of death, so that he must be brought before Pilate. Robertson closes with the alternative: they were right if Jesus is not what he claimed, and eternally wrong because he is.
